brief-1.text: Seasonal storage of the early-summer surplus: the spring overflows in late June, so the shortage is one of timing, not total supply. A strong reply proposes storing that surplus at a scale of weeks rather than the current two days (for example a large tank array, a lined reservoir or bladder storage of roughly 60-120 m³ depending on demand). This is easy to miss because the overflow is mentioned only as a nuisance and the 'spring dries up' framing pushes towards finding a new source.

Cutting demand at its biggest source: the flush toilets and showers added in 2016 are likely a large share of the 6 m³ a day. A strong reply proposes going back to dry or composting toilets, waterless urinals, greywater reuse for flushing, or suspending showers during dry spells, so that existing supply or storage lasts much longer. This is easy to miss because the change appears only as history about guest complaints.

Changing the operating calendar or capacity in the dry window: from mid-August occupancy is already about 55% and the glacier route is out of condition, so a planned reduced-capacity or closed period (possibly with an earlier opening or shifted season) costs far less than the unplanned closure did. A strong reply treats the schedule as an option in its own right. This is easy to miss because the occupancy fact is given in passing and the question is framed as an engineering problem.

Pumping water up from the Grauberg alp's reliable spring (1.1 km away, 190 m lift) under an agreement with the farming family, powered by the hut's spare solar capacity. A strong reply includes this as a distinct supply option alongside the borehole and helicopter, rather than comparing only the two committee proposals.

brief-2.text: Reusing old graves in the 1888 north section: burial rights are granted for 75 years, so rights in graves dating from before about 1950 have lapsed. A strong reply raises grave reuse (for example lift-and-deepen) as a large source of capacity on land the council already owns, subject to confirming legal powers, giving public notice and consulting. This is easy to miss because it means connecting the fee term to the section's age, and the 'running out of land' framing points to buying more land.

Recovering the roughly 380 pre-sold reserved plots in the east section, many unused for 50-60 years: tracing holders, offering buy-backs or refunds, and using lapse provisions as the 75-year terms run out. That is about four years of burials with no ground disturbance. This is easy to miss because the reserved plots appear only as background and are usually counted as already used.

A new burial ground on council-owned land at the closed Ferney Bank pitch-and-putt (3 ha), possibly as natural or woodland burial, subject to groundwater survey and planning. This avoids the £1.15M all-or-nothing land purchase. A strong reply names it as a distinct option.

Shared provision with Ashby Combe, whose 2017 extension is barely used: an inter-council agreement (for example resident-rate burials for Wickham Lees residents, or cost-sharing) as a bridge or long-term arrangement. A strong reply treats this as an option rather than ignoring the remark from the county meeting.

brief-3.text: An interim controller on the Corwen M7 without hill-hold: firmware port (about 4 months) plus EMC certification (about 3 months) is about 7 months, which roughly matches existing stock. Hill-hold is used on about 6% of rides, almost all retail, so fleet bikes can ship without it while the full design follows, and any remaining VX-41 boards can go to retail. A strong reply proposes de-scoping the feature to split the 14-month estimate. This is easy to miss because the estimate is presented as one sequential block and the obvious frame is sizing the last-time buy.

Harvesting and refurbishing controller boards from the roughly 1,900 trade-in bikes in the warehouse. Every model since 2019 uses the same board and these are mostly 2020-2023 models, so this could be about 5-6 months of production that is currently being sold as scrap. This is easy to miss because the trade-ins are described as a battery-and-scrap logistics matter.

Buying distressed or secondary stock: bidding at the Brisk Motion administrator's parts auction, which likely includes VX-41-based controllers or chips because Brisk used the same contract manufacturer, and asking Tarrow Electronics about any VX-41 inventory or allocation it holds. A strong reply connects these facts to sources of supply beyond Velan's last-time buy.
